blocks.content: Every process on a computer can be paused mid instruction and resumed later as if nothing happened. That trick is only possible because the operating system keeps a small record for each process that captures everything about its current state. That record is the process control block, or PCB. It is best thought of as the process ID card and memory combined into one data structure, the single place the kernel looks to remember who a process is and exactly what it was doing.

This chapter explains what a PCB actually is, walks through the fields it typically contains and why each one is needed, shows precisely how it powers context switching, explains where it lives in memory and who is allowed to touch it, clears up a common misconception, and covers how to talk about it in an interview.
1. Introduction: The Process ID Card and Memory
blocks.text: 1. Introduction: The Process ID Card and Memory

blocks.content: When you open three browser tabs, a music player, and a code editor at the same time, your computer is not actually running all of them at once on a single processor core. It is rapidly switching between them, giving each one a small slice of time before moving to the next. For that switching to feel seamless, the operating system must be able to stop a process at any point, put it aside, run something else, and later bring the first process back exactly where it left off, down to the last instruction and the last value sitting in a register.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A process control block is a data structure the kernel maintains for every process, holding all the information needed to describe that process current state so the operating system can manage, pause, and resume it correctly.

Without such a record, pausing a process would mean losing it. The operating system would have no way of knowing where the process was in its execution, what its variables looked like in the registers, or which files it had open. The PCB is what makes multitasking possible at all.
2. What the PCB Actually Is

A process control block is not a file you can open or a structure the programmer writes. It is an internal kernel data structure, typically implemented as a structure or record in the operating system source code itself. The moment a process is created, the kernel allocates a PCB for it, fills in the initial details, and keeps that PCB updated for as long as the process exists.
One PCB per process, always

Every single process on the system, whether it is a background service, a browser tab, or a small utility script, has exactly one PCB associated with it. The operating system keeps these PCBs organized, often linked together in queues that represent scheduling states, such as a ready queue or a waiting queue. When a process moves from one state to another, the operating system does not move the actual process code around, it simply updates the state field in that process PCB and relinks it into a different queue.

The PCB is the operating system representation of a process. If a piece of information is not in the PCB, as far as scheduling and context switching are concerned, the operating system does not know it.
3. The Fields Inside a PCB

The exact layout of a PCB differs between operating systems, but nearly all of them include the same core set of fields, because they all need to solve the same problem. Each field exists to answer a specific question the operating system will need to ask later.
Process ID

A unique number assigned to the process when it is created. Process names are not reliable identifiers because two processes can share a name, and a process can even rename itself. The process ID gives the kernel, other processes, and system calls a single unambiguous way to refer to this exact process, for example when sending it a signal or looking up its entry in a table.
Process state

The current stage the process is in, typically one of new, ready, running, waiting, or terminated. The scheduler relies entirely on this field to decide what to do with a process. A process marked ready sits in line for the CPU, one marked waiting is parked aside until an event such as disk input completes, and the scheduler never even glances at a terminated process.
Program counter

The memory address of the next instruction this process should execute. This is arguably the single most important field for resuming a process correctly. When the process is paused, its program counter is copied out and saved; when it runs again, that saved address is loaded back into the actual hardware program counter so execution continues from precisely the right spot rather than starting over or jumping somewhere wrong.
CPU registers

A snapshot of the values held in the processor registers, including general purpose registers, the stack pointer, and condition or status flags, at the exact instant the process was last interrupted. Knowing where to resume is not enough; the process also needs its intermediate calculations back exactly as they were. A partially computed sum sitting in a register, or a stack pointer marking the top of local variables, must be restored precisely or the program would behave incorrectly the moment it resumed.
CPU scheduling information

Details the scheduler needs to decide when this process should get the CPU relative to every other process, such as its priority, pointers to scheduling queues, and any scheduling parameters the algorithm in use requires. Without this, the scheduler would have no fair or informed basis for choosing who runs next.
Memory management information

Information describing which region of memory belongs to this process, such as base and limit register values, or page table and segment table references depending on the memory scheme the operating system uses. This lets the memory manager translate the addresses the process uses internally into the correct physical memory locations, and stops one process from ever reading or writing another process memory by accident.
Accounting information

Bookkeeping data such as how much CPU time the process has consumed so far, time limits, and any process or job identifiers used for tracking. Operating systems use this for monitoring system load, enforcing quotas, and in some environments for billing.
I/O status information

A record of the resources the process currently holds, such as the list of open files and the input or output devices allocated to it. The operating system needs this so it can correctly resume pending input and output operations when the process runs again, and so it can cleanly release every resource the process was holding the moment the process terminates.

4. The PCB and Context Switching

Context switching is the operating system act of stopping one running process and starting another on the same processor core, and the PCB is the mechanism that makes it safe. The switch is really just a careful save and restore performed against two PCBs.

["The timer interrupts, or the running process blocks on I/O, signalling that a switch is needed.","The operating system takes the current values sitting in the actual CPU registers and the program counter and copies them into the PCB of process A, the current, running process.","The operating system updates the state field for process A, for example from running to ready or waiting, and places its PCB into the appropriate queue.","The scheduler picks the next process to run, process B, and locates its PCB.","The operating system copies the saved register values and program counter out of the PCB for process B and loads them into the actual CPU registers.","The state for process B is set to running, and the processor resumes executing exactly where B left off the last time it was paused."]
items: The timer interrupts, or the running process blocks on I/O, signalling that a switch is needed.
The operating system takes the current values sitting in the actual CPU registers and the program counter and copies them into the PCB of process A, the current, running process.
The operating system updates the state field for process A, for example from running to ready or waiting, and places its PCB into the appropriate queue.
The scheduler picks the next process to run, process B, and locates its PCB.
The operating system copies the saved register values and program counter out of the PCB for process B and loads them into the actual CPU registers.
The state for process B is set to running, and the processor resumes executing exactly where B left off the last time it was paused.

blocks.content: Notice the symmetry. Everything that leaves the CPU goes into a PCB, and everything that enters the CPU comes from a PCB. Nothing about a process instructions or data actually moves during a context switch, only this small snapshot of register and bookkeeping values travels between the hardware and the PCB. That is precisely why a process can be interrupted in the middle of a single instruction sequence and later continue as though no time had passed for it at all.

blocks.title: Why this feels instantaneous to the process
blocks.content: From the point of view of process A, it simply executed one instruction after another. It has no way of sensing the gap where the CPU was busy running other processes, because every register it depends on was restored to exactly the value it expects.
5. Where the PCB Lives

The PCB itself lives in memory that only the kernel can access, generally described as protected or kernel space, and never in the ordinary memory region a user process reads and writes. This separation is deliberate and important.

blocks.title: Why a process cannot touch its own PCB
blocks.content: If an ordinary process could reach into its own PCB and edit fields like its priority, its memory limits, or its process state, it could cheat the scheduler into giving itself unfair CPU time, expand its own memory permissions, or fake its state to dodge termination. Keeping the PCB in protected kernel memory, reachable only through system calls the kernel controls, is what keeps scheduling and security decisions trustworthy.

This is also why looking up information about a running process, for example through a command line tool, never reads the PCB directly. Instead, the request goes through the kernel, which reads the real PCB internally and hands back only the specific, safe information the caller asked for.
6. Common Misconceptions
A few misunderstandings about the PCB come up often enough that they are worth calling out directly.

["Thinking the PCB is something the process itself creates or manages. It is not. It is purely an operating system data structure that lives in kernel memory, and the process it describes has no direct access to it at all.","Thinking the PCB is the process. The PCB only describes the process, in the same way an ID card describes a person without being that person. The actual running code and data of the process live elsewhere in memory.","Thinking the PCB only matters during a context switch. It is also consulted constantly by the scheduler, by system calls that report process information, and by the kernel when cleaning up a terminated process."]
items: Thinking the PCB is something the process itself creates or manages. It is not. It is purely an operating system data structure that lives in kernel memory, and the process it describes has no direct access to it at all.

Thinking the PCB is the process. The PCB only describes the process, in the same way an ID card describes a person without being that person. The actual running code and data of the process live elsewhere in memory.

Thinking the PCB only matters during a context switch. It is also consulted constantly by the scheduler, by system calls that report process information, and by the kernel when cleaning up a terminated process.

blocks.content: 7. The Interview Angle

A very common interview question pairs the process control block with context switching, asking you to explain step by step what specifically gets saved and restored when the operating system switches from one process to another. The strong answer is precise rather than vague: name the program counter and the full set of CPU register values as the two things that must be saved out of the CPU into the outgoing process PCB, and loaded back from the incoming process PCB into the CPU, and explain that this save and restore pair is exactly what allows a process to be paused mid instruction and resumed later with no visible disruption to it.

If you can explain the PCB and context switching together, using the save into the old PCB and restore from the new PCB framing, you are demonstrating a real understanding of how multitasking works underneath, not just a memorized definition.
